name: Substance-Field Analysis (TRIZ)
description: Model the interaction as an S1-S2-field triangle and apply Altshuller's 76 standard solutions
whenToUse: When an action between two substances is too weak, too strong, harmful or missing altogether and the matching TRIZ standard solutions are to be found; not to resolve a contradiction between two parameters — that is what the contradiction matrix is for.

situation.partial: S1 or S2 missing — please name both substances.
situation.incomplete: Incomplete model (no field) — a new interaction must be built.
situation.complete-useful: Complete, useful — improvement & next-generation jump possible.
situation.complete-insufficient: Complete but insufficient — strengthen or dynamise the field.
situation.complete-excessive: Complete but excessive — damp the action / self-limit.
situation.complete-harmful: Complete but harmful — destroy or neutralise the Su-Field.

problemNotePlaceholder: Optional: context, boundary conditions, cross-reference to 9-Windows / IFR / matrix …

1.name: Building / destroying Su-Field models
1.description: For incomplete models (1.1 synthesis) or harmful interactions (1.2 destruction).

2.name: Developing Su-Field models
2.description: For complete models with insufficient or improvable action — transition to complex, dynamic or ferromagnetic Su-Fields.

3.name: Transition to supersystem / microlevel
3.description: When the system reaches its limits — bi-/poly-system or jump to the microlevel.

4.name: Detection & measurement
4.description: Measurement / control problems — avoid measurement, measure indirectly, ferromagnetic detection.

5.name: Helper standards
5.description: Simplification and ideality — use existing substances / fields, phase changes, self-controlled transitions.

standardNotePlaceholder: How does this standard apply to the case at hand?

invariants.knownNotes: A note belongs to one of the 78 standard solutions.
invariants.knownSelections: A mark belongs to one of the 78 standard solutions.
invariants.validExpandedClasses: Only the classes 1 to 5 are expanded, each at most once.

1.title: Synthesis of a Su-Field model
1.description: When the interaction is weak or unknown and the model is incomplete, add the missing element (substance or field).
1.trigger: Incomplete Su-Field (one of the three elements is missing).
1.example: If two workpieces need to be glued, the field is missing — add heat (thermal field) so the adhesive cures.

2.title: Inner complex Su-Field
2.description: When the object’s properties block a classical Su-Field, modify S2 internally by adding an auxiliary substance.
2.trigger: S2 resists direct interaction; properties cannot be changed directly.
2.example: Steel that cannot be bent — soften from inside by hydrogen embedding (hydriding).

3.title: Outer complex Su-Field
3.description: When S2 cannot be changed internally, attach an auxiliary substance externally (coating, additive).
3.trigger: S2 must not be modified, but a surface coating is acceptable.
3.example: Workpiece with a non-stick coating instead of changing the material.

4.title: Su-Field synthesis using the environment
4.description: Use a substance already present in the environment as S1 or mediator.
4.trigger: A suitable substance already exists in the environment (air, water, dust).
4.example: Air cushion instead of mechanical rollers for low-friction motion.

5.title: Su-Field synthesis using modified environment
5.description: If the natural environment alone is insufficient, alter it chemically or physically.
5.trigger: Environment is available but too weak or unsuitable.
5.example: Replace the atmosphere with inert gas (argon) so the workpiece does not oxidise.

6.title: Maximum action where prohibited
6.description: When maximum field action is required but the field must not act on S2 directly, act on an intermediate carrier.
6.trigger: Direct maximum action would damage S2.
6.example: High-frequency welding via an intermediate carrier rather than directly on the sensitive part.

7.title: Selective field action
7.description: When the field should act with maximum effect in some regions and minimum in others, use a protective or modifying substance.
7.trigger: Inhomogeneous effect on S2 is required (e.g. local hardening).
7.example: Local induction hardening — field acts only on the induced region; the rest stays soft.

8.title: Ferromagnetic substance + magnetic field
8.description: Use a ferromagnetic substance and a magnetic field when ordinary fields cannot do the job.
8.trigger: Classical fields are insufficient; magnetic manipulation is possible.
8.example: Iron powder + magnetic field as a shape-adaptive tool.

1.title: Introducing a third substance to neutralise
1.description: When two substances interact harmfully, introduce a third substance that separates or neutralises them.
1.trigger: Harmful interaction between S1 and S2 is present.
1.example: Lubrication film between rubbing surfaces reduces wear.

2.title: Modification of one substance
2.description: Modify one of the two substances so the harmful interaction disappears.
2.trigger: Harmful interaction; modification of S1 or S2 is acceptable.
2.example: Anti-reflective coating on a lens — harmful reflection disappears.

3.title: Removing or diverting the harmful field
3.description: When a field causes a harmful effect, divert or shield it.
3.trigger: Harmful field between S1 and S2.
3.example: Faraday cage shields against electromagnetic interference.

4.title: Counter-field for neutralisation
4.description: Generate a counter-field that cancels the harmful field.
4.trigger: Harmful field; generating a counter-field is possible.
4.example: Active noise cancellation (ANC) — counter-sound nulls the noise.

5.title: Absorbing the harmful interaction via an auxiliary substance
5.description: Introduce a substance that absorbs the harmful interaction and renders it harmless.
5.trigger: Harmful effect should be absorbed (not just diverted).
5.example: Activated-carbon filter binds pollutants in exhaust gas.

1.title: Transition to a chain Su-Field
1.description: When a simple Su-Field is insufficient, chain several Su-Fields (S1 acts on S2 via S3).
1.trigger: Simple model too weak; an intermediate step is feasible.
1.example: Lever transmission: force → intermediate carrier → workpiece.

2.title: Transition to a double Su-Field
2.description: Use a second substance or a second field in parallel to amplify or specialise the action.
2.trigger: One action is insufficient; a complementary second action is needed.
2.example: Grinding wheel + coolant: mechanical + thermal field in parallel.

1.title: From uncontrolled to controlled field
1.description: Replace a hard-to-control field with a more controllable one (often electromagnetic).
1.trigger: Mechanical / chemical field is hard to meter.

2.title: Fragmenting a substance
2.description: Break a solid substance into smaller parts (powder, particles) for finer control.
2.trigger: Control over S1 or S2 needs to be more fine-grained.
2.example: Powder coating instead of a solid coating block — finer thickness control.

3.title: Transition to porous structure
3.description: Make a substance porous so it can hold fields and other substances.
3.trigger: Substance needs to buffer materials / heat / fields.
3.example: Porous sintered body as a heat store.

4.title: Dynamisation
4.description: Switch from a static to a moving system (rigid → jointed → elastic → fluid → field).
4.trigger: Static solution hits limits; adaptation to conditions is needed.

5.title: From constant to variable / pulsed field
5.description: Replace constant action with time-varying, pulsed or modulated action.
5.trigger: Constant action wastes energy or damages S2.
5.example: Pulsed instead of continuous laser for clean machining.

6.title: Structuring the field or substance
6.description: Add structure to the field or substance — spatial (pattern) or temporal (sequence).
6.trigger: Homogeneous action is suboptimal; structure raises efficiency.
6.example: Structured laser beams for holography or pattern generation.

1.title: Matching natural frequency
1.description: Tune the field frequency to the natural / resonance frequency of the object.
1.example: Ultrasonic cleaning: frequency tuned to cavitation bubbles.

2.title: Multiple frequencies for multiple tasks
2.description: If the system has several tasks, use different frequencies for each.
2.trigger: Multiple independent tasks should be served by one carrier.
2.example: Multiplexing — different frequency bands carry different signals in parallel.

3.title: Use pauses for other actions
3.description: During pauses of one action, other actions can run — no conflicts, shared resources.
3.trigger: Action does not run continuously; pauses are usable.
3.example: MRI sequences — different pulses between acquisition windows.

4.title: Matching an uncontrollable rhythm
4.description: When a rhythm cannot be controlled, align the system to its natural cadence.
4.trigger: External / natural rhythm is given (time of day, machine cycle).
4.example: Energy storage matches the natural pulsation of the PV plant.

5.title: Using resonance
5.description: Deliberately drive a resonance to maximise effect at minimal input energy.
5.trigger: Energy efficiency is critical; system can resonate.
5.example: Vibratory conveyor exploits resonance for low energy use.

1.title: Ferromagnetic material + magnetic field
1.description: Introduce ferromagnetic particles or parts controlled via a magnetic field.
1.trigger: Controllability via classical fields is insufficient.
1.example: Magneto-rheological fluid as adaptive shock-absorber fill.

2.title: Magnetic fluid (ferrofluid)
2.description: Use a liquid with suspended ferromagnetic particles for shape-free, field-controlled action.
2.trigger: Shape / position must be free and field-controllable.
2.example: Ferrofluid as a bearing seal in hard-disk drives.

3.title: Capillary porous structures with magnetic liquid
3.description: Combine magnetic liquid with capillary structures for directed transport.
3.trigger: Liquid transport must be directional and field-controlled.
3.example: Magnetically steered microfluidics in lab-on-a-chip devices.

4.title: Complex ferromagnetic Su-Field
4.description: Build a complex model with several ferromagnetic components.
4.example: Stacked magnetisation to create spatial patterns.

5.title: Additives in the environment
5.description: Distribute ferromagnetic additives into the environment to achieve the effect there.
5.trigger: Direct intervention on the workpiece is hard.
5.example: Magnetite tracers in a flow make the volume rate measurable.

6.title: Adding magnetic substance to the environment
6.description: When the environment itself is non-magnetic, make it magnetic.
6.trigger: Environment can be modified; magnetic separation is desired.
6.example: Magnetite enrichment of sludge for magnetic phase separation.

7.title: Using natural ferromagnetism
7.description: Check whether the environment already contains ferromagnetic substances (iron, steel).
7.example: Magnetic alignment of iron particles in lubricant for wear monitoring.

8.title: Using physical effects (Curie point, hysteresis)
8.description: Use physical effects such as the Curie temperature or magnetic hysteresis as a self-controlled switch.
8.trigger: Self-acting control at a threshold is needed.
8.example: Self-regulating heater cartridge: material loses its magnetism above the Curie point, reducing current.

9.title: Dynamising the ferromagnetic Su-Field
9.description: Move from a static ferromagnetic construction to a moving / variable one.
9.trigger: Static magnetic field insufficient; variability improves effect.
9.example: Rotating magnet creates a rotating field for contactless motors.

10.title: Structuring the magnetic field
10.description: Create deliberate spatial structures in the magnetic field (inhomogeneities, gradients).
10.example: Magnetic gradient fields in MRI for spatial encoding.

11.title: Rhythm matching in ferromagnetic systems
11.description: Tune magnetic pulse frequencies to the natural frequency of the ferromagnetic system.
11.trigger: Efficiency of the magnetic interaction must be maximised.
11.example: Resonant wireless charging: optimal frequency for maximum energy transfer.

12.title: Electric instead of magnetic field
12.description: When magnetic fields fail, replace them with an electric field or combine both.
12.example: Electrostatic powder coating instead of magnetic attraction.

1.title: Bi-system: pair two identical systems
1.description: Pair two identical systems for synergy.
1.trigger: Single system saturated; doubling brings new properties.
1.example: Double cutter — two parallel blades create finer cuts.

2.title: Poly-system: many identical systems
2.description: Combine many identical systems into a poly-system (array).
2.trigger: Massive parallelisation possible; individual unit insignificant.
2.example: LED matrix as headlight instead of a single lamp.

3.title: Differentiating bi- / poly-systems
3.description: Bi- / poly-systems become richer when their elements have differentiated (not identical) properties.
3.trigger: Bi- / poly-system with identical units saturates.
3.example: Stereo instead of mono — two speakers carrying different signals.

4.title: Combining opposite properties
4.description: Combine systems with opposite properties (hot + cold, hard + soft, black + white).
4.example: Sandwich part with a hard outer and a soft inner layer.

5.title: Folding — bi-system back into mono
5.description: When the bi-system has done its job, integrate the functionality into a single system.
5.trigger: Bi-system over-dimensioned; integration into one system possible.
5.example: Reversible Phillips + slot screwdriver bit head.

1.title: Transition to the microlevel
1.description: Replace macroscopic elements with microscopic / molecular / field solutions.
1.trigger: Macro system saturated; micro solution available.
1.example: Microfluidics replacing pump-hose systems for small flow rates.

1.title: Avoid measurement by changing the system
1.description: When something is hard to measure, change the system so measurement is no longer required.
1.example: Self-diagnostic sensors with threshold switches instead of measure + logic.

2.title: Use copies / models
2.description: Rather than measuring the original, measure a simpler model or copy.
2.trigger: Original system too complex or inaccessible.
2.example: Wind-tunnel model instead of full-scale aircraft.

3.title: Measure successive changes
3.description: Measure relative changes instead of absolute values — often more accurate and simpler.
3.trigger: Absolute measurement is hard; relative values are sufficient.
3.example: Comparator measurement against a reference (difference, not absolute).

1.title: Synthesise an indirect measuring Su-Field
1.description: When an effect cannot be measured directly, couple it to an easily measurable field.
1.example: Pressure measurement via membrane deformation (mechanical → electrical).

2.title: Inner complex measuring Su-Field
2.description: Modify the object so it itself emits information (e.g. fluoresces under load).

3.title: Outer complex measuring Su-Field
3.description: Attach a measurement marker externally (coating, applied sensor).
3.trigger: Object may not be internally modified.

4.title: Use the environment as a measurement carrier
4.description: Let the environment around the object carry the information (shadow, distortion, echo).
4.example: Radar measurement — the environment’s echo describes the object.

1.title: Use physical effects for measurement
1.description: Use physical effects (piezo, Doppler, Hall) to convert a quantity into an electrical signal.
1.trigger: Mechanical / chemical measurement should be electrified.
1.example: Doppler effect for speed measurement (radar, ultrasonic probe).

2.title: Use resonance for measurement
2.description: Natural frequency or resonance of a part reveals its state.
2.example: Tuning-fork frequency measures liquid level / density.

3.title: Resonance of an associated object
3.description: When the main object is hard to measure, measure an associated object with coupled resonance.
3.trigger: Direct measurement on S2 hard; associated object available.
3.example: Cavitation bubble resonance measures ultrasound intensity indirectly.

1.title: Magnetic field + ferromagnetism for measurement
1.description: Use magnetic fields and ferromagnetic materials as the measuring element.
1.example: Hall sensor measures current via its induced magnetic field.

2.title: Magnetically marked indicators
2.description: Attach a ferromagnetic marker to the part of interest and detect it.
2.trigger: Position / motion of a part must be measured contactlessly.
2.example: Speed measurement with a toothed wheel + Hall sensor.

3.title: Magnetic substance + Curie point for temperature
3.description: Use the Curie point of a ferromagnetic material as a self-acting temperature threshold.
3.trigger: Temperature switching at a precise threshold desired.
3.example: Magnet switch that drops out above the Curie temperature.

4.title: Structuring in magnetic measurement
4.description: Create magnetic gradients / patterns to encode spatial information.
4.trigger: Spatial resolution of the measurement is required.
4.example: MRI — gradient fields encode location in frequency.

5.title: Rhythm matching in magnetic measurement
5.description: Tune measurement pulses to the inherent dynamics of the magnetic system (Larmor frequency etc.).
5.trigger: Efficiency / sensitivity of measurement must be maximised.
5.example: Larmor resonance in NMR — pulse sequence matches the natural frequency of nuclear spins.

1.title: Transition bi → poly in measurement
1.description: Multiple sensors in parallel — averaging, error correction, spatial coverage.
1.trigger: Single sensor is unreliable or one-dimensional.
1.example: Sensor array (multiple microphones, redundant Hall sensors).

2.title: Evolution of measurement systems
2.description: Measurement systems evolve from simple → complex → intelligent (auto-calibrating, learning).
2.example: Smart sensor with self-calibration and drift compensation.

1.title: Indirect: use an existing substance
1.description: Use a substance already present rather than introducing a new one.
1.example: Use the workpiece’s own chips as a brush.

2.title: Substance appears only when needed
2.description: A substance is generated only locally / temporarily — not present permanently.
2.trigger: Permanent existence of the substance would be problematic.
2.example: Ice as a temporary tool that disappears after use.

3.title: Substance disappears after use
3.description: Consumable that dissolves, evaporates or degrades after doing its job.

4.title: Inflatable / hollow / foam structures
4.description: Use minimum mass by building the system inflatable / hollow / foamed.
4.example: Airbag — huge volume from minimal material.

1.title: Use an existing field from the environment
1.description: Rather than generating a field, use one already present (Earth’s magnetism, gravity, solar radiation).
1.trigger: Energy saving; ambient field is usable.

2.title: Generate fields from environmental substances
2.description: Generate a field from existing substances (combustion, evaporation).
2.trigger: External energy input should be avoided.
2.example: Self-heating meal — chemical reaction generates heat from reagents.

3.title: Ferromagnetic substance + magnetic field helper
3.description: As a fallback, drop in a mini-Su-Field of ferromagnet + magnetic field.
3.example: Magnetic chip collector in drilling coolant.

1.title: Phase transition for new properties
1.description: Use phase changes (solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas) for stepwise property changes.
1.trigger: A property should change suddenly / drastically.
1.example: Latent heat storage — phase change at constant temperature.

2.title: Dual properties at phase transitions
2.description: Phase transitions often combine two properties (transition zone).
2.example: Water vapour at 100 °C: condenses AND evaporates — heat is held.

3.title: Physical effects at phase transitions
3.description: Use volume, heat or conductivity changes at phase transitions as function carriers.
3.trigger: Effect at the phase change is usable.
3.example: Bimetallic switch uses differential thermal expansion.

4.title: Two-phase system
4.description: System with two stable phases — properties controlled by phase choice.

5.title: Interaction between phases
5.description: Engineer deliberate interactions between coexisting phases (evaporative cooling etc.).
5.trigger: Phases coexist; their interaction is usable.
5.example: Evaporative cooling — vaporisation removes heat from the liquid.

1.title: Self-controlled transitions (Curie, hysteresis, saturation)
1.description: Use physical effects that let the system respond to thresholds on its own.
1.trigger: Self-acting response to a condition desired.

2.title: Combine effects for stronger action
2.description: Combine several physical effects in series / parallel for a strong total effect.
2.example: Piezo effect + resonance generates high voltage from mechanical vibration (energy harvesting).

1.title: Self-service
1.description: The system performs a function on its own, with no external input (cf. IFR-1).

2.title: Particle generation by decomposition
2.description: Generate new substances by decomposing existing ones (electrolysis, photolysis, pyrolysis).
2.trigger: A specific substance is needed locally.
2.example: Oxygen produced from water by electrolysis.

3.title: Particle generation by combination
3.description: Combine existing substances / particles into a new substance with desired properties.
3.trigger: New substance with specific properties required.
3.example: Powder-bed processes — particles sinter into a solid.
